blocks.text: This Is Class War
The latest on the student protests in France, the art world’s AI problem, one-on-one with Rosana Paulino, and Beer With a Painter featuring Melissa Brown.

The subway car rattles, shakes, and screeches as it tunnels us from Brooklyn to Manhattan underneath the East River. I hold on tight to a pole, while my eyes are fixed on an ad for the Broadway musical Les Misérables .

My social media feed shows me only looting and vandalism in France, painting a violent picture of the largely peaceful student protests. Panicking, the art world’s blue-chip class shuts down Art Basel Paris early and flees the city. The Louvre also closes to protect its treasures. Loot a little and they throw you in jail; loot a lot and they let you open a museum.

I get to a benefit dinner for an art residency held in a former bank. A peppy auctioneer asks the who’s who to open their hearts and wallets. Paddles go up and down, and a donation ticker on a big screen climbs to astronomical numbers while I admire the building’s huge stained-glass skylight. Up there, near a golden clock that no longer ticks, an inscription in marble letters reads, "It's what we save rather than what we earn that ensures a competence for the future."

Outside, Midtown Manhattan is huffing and puffing, and the neon lights glow too bright. A sign in a bodega window advertises that the Powerball jackpot has hit $650 million, and I drift into a daydream about what my life would be like if I won that much money. I picture myself raising the paddle at auctions and amassing a serious art collection — just to support artists, you know.

I sit somewhere for a coffee and see the barista trying to buy a ticket on her phone for a new movie about white-collar convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes, who’s become a cultural icon among the petite bourgeoisie. The barista can’t find a ticket because the theater is sold out.

On the subway ride back home, I get sucked into an essay about Kazimir Malevich’s concept of the “White Abyss” and miss my stop by several stations, adding an hour to my commute. I get off in an impoverished neighborhood and see that someone has graffitied “Class War” all over a residential building. There’s nothing open but a convenience store at a gas station. Fuck it, I’m buying a Powerball ticket.
—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief
Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI

links.text: Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI

blocks.text: Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia. | Valentina Di Liscia
